The CB Weekly Market Recap (Oct 4th - Oct 10th, 2026) ⚡️ 

 🔴 All three major indices finished the week higher. The S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,811.54 for a gain of 1.15%, with the Dow at 51,654.95 up 0.93% and the Nasdaq at 27,366.17 up 0.64%. The S&P set a record of 7,844.52 on Tuesday before easing back. That was the Dow’s biggest weekly gain since early August and the Nasdaq’s fourth consecutive weekly advance, its first such run since the streak that ended in May.

 🔴 The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.364% on Wednesday, its highest level since April 2002. The 30-year reached 5.70%, also a 24-year high. The average 30-year fixed mortgage jumped from 7.30% to 7.49% on the back of it. Yields eased back toward 5.2% by Thursday, which is what gave equities the room to recover into Friday.

 🔴 Treasury’s $39 billion 10-year auction on Wednesday drew strong demand at a yield of 5.30%. That is the highest yield on any US 10-year sale since November 2000. This is not a US-only story either, with UK 30-year gilts at their highest since 1998, France’s 10-year approaching 5% and Japan’s 10-year at 3.11%, a three-decade high. We also saw bond funds take in roughly $26.4 billion over the five days to October 1st, so these yields are pulling income buyers back in.

 🔴 Tech sold off hard on Thursday after the Financial Times reported that OpenAI’s annualised revenue sits around $50 billion rather than the $70 billion widely cited. The Nasdaq-100 fell 1.4% and chip stocks dropped 3.4%, with Nvidia off 2.9%, Intel 5.3% and Oracle 5.5%. The gap comes down to accounting, as Anthropic books the full value of cloud partner sales while OpenAI records only its own share. OpenAI still told investors it expects to reach $70 billion by the end of 2026.

 🔴 WTI settled Friday at $91.85 and Brent at $104.72, leaving them up roughly 0.8% and 2.4% on the week. Thursday did most of that work, with Brent jumping 4.1% and WTI 3.6% on Middle East supply fears and the Gulf hurricane. Friday gave a little back after Trump said the US would not strike Iran before the November 3rd midterms. Brent holding above $100 on that news tells you how much supply risk is still priced into the Gulf.

 🔴 Hurricane Isaias shut in about 1.3 million barrels a day of US Gulf of Mexico production, roughly 63% of the total. The storm threatened Chevron’s Pascagoula refinery in Mississippi and Vertex’s Saraland plant in Alabama, though it appeared to veer away from the dense refining belt in southern Louisiana. Gulf Coast refineries are already running at 95% of capacity, so there is no slack to absorb a loss. Any plant that does go down would take one to two weeks to restart.

 🔴 US diesel inventories are at their lowest level for this time of year since the EIA began reporting in 1982. Average retail diesel sat near $6.28 a gallon, about 70% above where it was before the war with Iran began. NYMEX diesel futures did fall 2.9% on Friday to around $4.74 a gallon after Trump cleared Russian diesel for world markets. That helps the product side but does nothing for the Gulf shipping shortfall underneath it.

 🔴 Bitcoin closed the week near $82,500, down roughly 4%. It fell as low as $80,427 on Thursday before recovering, having been rejected just below $87,400 earlier in the month. Ether took the heavier damage, dropping more than 7% to below $2,500, with Solana at $110 and XRP at $1.39 after similar falls. Total crypto market cap slipped to about $2.92 trillion, and forced liquidations hit roughly $548 million on Wednesday alone.

 🔴 Spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $484.9 million on Wednesday, their largest single-day outflow since June. That erased the $321.6 million which had come in over October’s first four sessions and flipped the month negative. Ether ETFs have now run eight consecutive sessions of outflows, with $542 million leaving in the week to October 9th, their worst week since late January. We also saw combined Bitcoin and Ether ETF outflows approach $1 billion for October as a whole.

 🔴 As for next week, September CPI lands on Wednesday and it decides whether the Fed can comfortably hold on October 28th. Major US banks start reporting on Tuesday, which gives the first real read on how businesses and consumers are absorbing these borrowing costs. Watch the hurricane’s track through the refining belt as well, because diesel has no cushion left to give. Stay sharp lads.

Trader alleges Papertrade exploit via Hyperliquid BBO manipulation

X user Boblob alleged that two wallets exploited Papertrade’s pricing mechanism by using roughly $20 million orders on Hyperliquid to move ETH quotes by 10–20 basis points while holding much larger long positions on Papertrade. The HyperEVM-based perpetual platform reportedly uses the midpoint of Hyperliquid’s best bid and offer as its execution price, making it potentially sensitive to short-term BBO manipulation. Trader Rune noted that Papertrade’s own documentation lists BBO manipulation as an unresolved protocol risk. The allegations have not been independently verified, and Papertrade has not confirmed any losses. — link

Ledger confirms hardware implant attack, says systems not breached

Ledger said an unauthorized hardware implant was found inside an affected device, confirming physical tampering. The company said there is no evidence its own infrastructure, systems or services were compromised, while distributor CryptoBilis has suspended hardware wallet sales. Ledger advised affected users to avoid initializing unused devices and consider moving assets to wallets created with new recovery phrases. Earlier on-chain analysis estimated losses linked to the incident at more than $86 million. — link

XRPL fixes decade-old bug that could have minted trillions of XRP

RippleX and the XRP Ledger Foundation disclosed that a critical payment-engine overflow bug could have allowed an attacker to create spendable XRP beyond the network’s fixed supply using a specially crafted transaction. The issue, present in code dating back to 2015, was reported through the XRPL bug bounty program and fixed in xrpld 3.4.1 on September 25, with more than 80% of default validators upgraded that day.

Security researcher @Cayden_Liao said his team’s proof of concept could mint about 18 trillion XRP in a single transaction, roughly 184 times XRP’s intended 100 billion supply, and earned the program’s maximum $250,000 bounty. XRPL said it found no evidence the flaw was ever exploited on a public network. — link

AI companies are borrowing LESS as investors grow wary of the $466 BILLION debt boom.

AI-related borrowing PLUNGED nearly 80%, from a record $113 BILLION in June to just $23 BILLION in September.

That's a $90 BILLION decline in THREE months, according to Morgan Stanley data cited by FT.

“Everybody’s being tapped and everybody’s getting a bit tighter,” Sona Asset Management's John Aylward told the FT.

But is LESS borrowing necessarily bad?

Not entirely. Slower borrowing could be a HEALTHY correction, allowing companies to manage debt while investors reassess risks.

However, if lenders are losing confidence in AI's profitability, tighter financing could delay data centers, weaken chip demand, and pressure tech valuations.

The implications could extend beyond AI to corporate credit and the broader stock market.

 Star Xu: Hyperliquid's Matching Engine Is More Market Maker Friendly 

OKX founder Star Xu said on the New Era Finance Podcast that Hyperliquid differs fundamentally from centralized order book exchanges in its technical design. While centralized exchanges process orders individually, Hyperliquid matches orders block by block and prioritizes cancellations within each block, allowing market makers to cancel orders ahead of takers. He believes this market maker friendly design explains why Hyperliquid's order book depth appears better than that of many centralized exchanges, while offering another approach for long-tail assets with limited liquidity. — link

🛡 Is Your Hardware Wallet Still Safe? 🛡 

Buying from an authorised reseller and passing an authenticity check should give you some confidence in a hardware wallet.

The latest Ledger incident shows why this isn't a guarantee.

On 10 October, Ledger confirmed an unauthorised hardware implant in a device linked to its CryptoBilis investigation. Researchers have reported tens of millions of dollars in suspected losses, though Ledger hasn’t confirmed the total.

Then, on 11 October, a phishing post appeared on Coldcard’s official X account, directing users to a fake wallet-migration site. Even checking the official account wouldn’t have been enough to spot the scam.

So, is a hardware wallet still the safe option? To find out, we went through every hardware wallet incident of 2026 and looked at where each one actually broke.

 🧩 Where Hardware Wallets Broke In 2026 

Notably, of this year's incidents where people actually lost money or personal data, only one came from a flaw in the device itself. The rest went after everything around it.

 ▪️ The shop : the Ledger implant, found in a device sold by CryptoBilis, a Southeast Asian reseller on Ledger's authorised list.

 ▪️ The customer list : a breach at Trezor's shipping provider exposed the names and home addresses of 80,689 customers, and a flaw in SafePal's order-tracking plug-in exposed around 39,800 more.

 ▪️ The inbox : in September, a breach at email platform Brevo let attackers send a fake "Critical Security Alert" from Trezor's real account.

 ▪️ The search bar : a Google sponsored ad for "Trezor wallet" in August, and a fake Ledger site sitting at the top of Google this month.

 ▪️ The device itself : a firmware bug meant Coldcards had been generating weak seeds since 2021. Analysts have counted between $111 million and $116 million stolen.

In other words, the secure chip at the heart of these devices has mostly held up. What failed was the shop, the shipping list, the email and the search results.

 🔍 Why The Authenticity Check Didn't Help 

For context, Ledger's Genuine Check works by asking the device's secure chip to sign a challenge with a key only Ledger's factory could have installed. That proves the chip is real. However, Ledger’s own security documentation explicitly says physical spying implants can escape detection if the original secure element remains intact.

The implant in this case appears to sit in that gap. According to Mark Karpelès, the former Mt. Gox CEO, whose implanted device came from Malaysia in flawless shrink wrap, the extra chip sat where the screen's padding should be. He says it recognised the setup screens and sent the seed phrase out over a mobile data connection. Ledger confirmed an "unauthorized hardware implant" in one victim's device on 10 October, and says every confirmed case so far involves CryptoBilis.

✅ The Checklist 

Here's everything you need to do to protect yourself.

 ➡️ Buy directly where possible. Use the manufacturer’s own store and avoid second-hand devices. Buying direct reduces the number of people handling your wallet before it reaches you; it doesn’t eliminate every risk.

 ➡️ Follow the setup checks for your exact model. Stop if the box contains a prewritten recovery phrase or a preset PIN. Sealed packaging alone isn’t proof that a device is safe.

 ➡️ Bookmark the official website. Use that bookmark for downloads and security notices. Don’t let a search ad, email or reply under a support post choose the destination for you.

 ➡️ Verify urgent warnings separately. If a message tells you to migrate immediately, open the vendor’s website yourself and cross-check the advisory through another official channel. The Coldcard incident shows why a familiar account name isn’t enough.

 ➡️ Keep your recovery phrase out of online forms and support conversations. A request to enter it to “secure” or “validate” your wallet is a reason to stop.

 ➡️ If your device lets you add your own randomness, use it . Coldcard says seeds created with at least 50 private dice rolls were not at risk from its bug.

 ‼️ If You Already Bought From CryptoBilis 

Ledger's advice is clear. If the device is still unused, don't set it up. If you've already set it up, move your funds to a new seed on a device bought directly from Ledger.

The same logic applies to Coldcard owners whose seed was generated on the affected firmware without dice rolls. Updating the firmware doesn't repair an existing seed, so the only fix is to create a new one and move your funds.

 ➖ ➖ ➖ ➖ 

 🧐 Bottom Line : A hardware wallet is still far safer than keeping your keys on a phone or an exchange. That said, 2026 has shown that attackers rarely go after the chip. They go after the shop you buy from, the company that ships it and the emails that follow. Buy direct, add your own dice rolls where you can, and never trust a message that tells you to move your funds. Stay safe out there.

💪 Crypto’s Gacha Trade: Who is Winning? 

Onchain gacha has become a substantial collectibles business, with leading platforms processing hundreds of millions of dollars in monthly pack purchases. 

But who is winning depends on what is measured 👇 

—-
 💲 The Selling Point: Real Collectibles, Instant Trading 

Onchain gacha platforms sell randomized digital packs backed by real, vaulted collectibles, typically graded trading cards. 

Buyers can keep their cards digitally, request physical delivery, resell them, or accept an instant buyback.

The appeal combines the excitement of opening packs with easier trading. 

A vaulted card can change owners without being shipped and authenticated each time. 

Instant buybacks also let customers exit immediately or recycle their proceeds into another pack.

That convenience drives activity, but creates an important distinction that pack spending measures transactions, not necessarily fresh money entering the market.

——
 🆚 Competitive Landscape: Two Leaders, and a Recovering Challenger 

July exposed differences between the major platforms. 

Combined pack spending fell -17.5% to $284.3 million, following June’s record. 

In a year Collector Crypt, Phygitals and Beezie contracted, while Courtyard and Monster grew. 

Courtyard alone sold more packs; Monster’s growth came from higher average prices. 

Phygitals is recovering, with 30-day pack spending roughly twice July’s $14.9 million. Beezie and Monster remain substantially below their totals. 

Competition is increasingly concentrated around the two leaders, with Phygitals the strongest smaller challenger by retained revenue. 

——-
 💻 Current Revenue: What Platforms Keep After Buybacks 

• Collector Crypt led pack spending over the latest 30-day period at $149 million, but Courtyard retained more revenue after buybacks: $22.9 million on $81 million in spending, compared with Collector Crypt’s $15.3 million. 

• Phygitals followed with $30.7 million in spending and $5.67 million in retained revenue. 

• Beezie and Monster were considerably smaller, retaining $170,000 and $158,000 on spending of $8.06 million and $3.25 million, respectively. 

Across six tracked platforms, including Bonkuji, revenue after buybacks totaled $44.17 million, including relevant marketplace income, per Blockworks.

The gap between spending and retained revenue reflects the importance of buybacks. 

• In July, platforms returned $249.4 million, or 87.7% of pack spending, to customers, leaving $34.9 million before further costs. 

Customers can reuse those proceeds to purchase more packs, allowing the same money to generate multiple transactions without equivalent fresh demand. 

Revenue after buybacks is therefore a more useful measure than gross spending, but it is not profit . 

Card costs, grading, custody, fulfillment, payment processing and operating expenses still need to be covered.

——-
 🏆 Current Leaders: A Comparison 

• Courtyard generates roughly 50% more retained revenue on just over half Collector Crypt’s pack spending. Its latest secondary-market volume was also higher: $6.53 million versus $5.09 million. 

• Courtyard averaged 6,556 daily active users, versus Collector Crypt’s 871. 

• Credit cards funded 34.2% of Courtyard’s pack spending, compared with roughly 1% at Collector Crypt, indicating broader access beyond crypto-native customers. Its lower effective buyback offer also boosts retained revenue, while giving customers less when they sell back. 

• Collector Crypt’s strengths are distribution and large buyers. 
Pine Analytics reported $433.5 million in third-quarter gross sales, up 8% from the previous quarter. 

However, monthly sales fell from $212.2 million in June to $134.5 million in September, and 548 wallets supplied 83% of quarterly pack spending. 

The scale is substantial yet customer concentration remains a weakness.
———

⏩ Forward Outlook: 

The underlying collector market extends well beyond crypto. GemRate estimated $2.62 billion in eBay trading-card singles sales in 2025, excluding sealed products, lots and sets.

July research placed onchain platforms at 1.12% of a $702.6 million monthly card-resale market. 

Holding that market constant, a 5–10% share would represent $422–843 million in annual secondary trading. This is an illustrative scenario, not a forecast or platform revenue estimate. 

Incumbents are already competing. GameStop publicly launched digital Power Packs on April 15, offering $25–$2,500 packs, PSA-vaulted cards and instant sellbacks. The product’s appeal is available to businesses with established retail distribution. GameStop announcement

——-
 🔖 Bottom Line 

Courtyard leads in retained revenue, Collector Crypt in spending, and Phygitals is recovering. The lasting winner will need repeat collectors, independent resale demand and disciplined inventory costs.

🤖 THE GOOGLE GEMINI PLAYBOOK 

Gemini becomes more useful when you give it something specific to work with, like the email containing your booking, the document outlining your project, or the calendar showing your actual availability.

For people already using Google’s apps, that connection is the attraction. Hands-on Workspace examples show the practical value of bringing emails and documents into the same conversation.

Gemini deserves a closer look and here's a practical guide with prompts 👇 

——
 1. Connect Gemini to your Google life 

• Sign in to Gemini with the account containing your emails and files. 

• Open Connected Apps on the current web interface, look under Customize → Connectors and connect Google Workspace. 

You can also type @ in a conversation and select an app to begin connecting it. Google’s connection guide
Start with something you can easily verify:

 Find my latest Gmail conversation with [PERSON] about [PROJECT]. Summarise the agreed actions, deadlines, and unanswered questions. 

• Link the emails you used, and flag anything a newer message changed.

• Mention the service, person, project, and timeframe explicitly. 

Google recommends identifying Workspace content through keywords and app names rather than pasting document URLs. Work and school accounts may require administrator access. 

——
 2. Give it Context Worth Remembering 

Under Settings & help → Personal Intelligence → Instructions for Gemini, save the preferences you otherwise repeat in every conversation. Instructions setup

 I work in [ROLE], in [LOCATION/TIMEZONE]. Lead with the answer. Keep routine responses under 200 words. Separate facts from assumptions. When information is missing, ask only questions that could materially change the result. 

Eligible personal accounts can also connect services such as Search and YouTube for more personalised responses. 

This depends on your settings and availability; Gemini does not automatically see everything associated with your Google account. 

• One setting deserves attention: Workspace connections require Keep Activity. With it enabled, Google can use saved activity to improve its services, including AI models. Review that choice before connecting sensitive material.

—-
 3. Build one assistant for a task you repeat 

A useful first Gem has a narrow job: weekly updates, meeting preparation, or editing client emails.

• Open Gems → New Gem, add instructions, and attach relevant files under Knowledge. 

A good example of the finished output is particularly useful. Drive files added to a Gem reflect subsequent changes to those files. 

Try a Weekly Update Editor:

 Turn my notes into Completed, Next, and Blockers. Preserve names, dates, and numbers. Never invent progress. Highlight missing owners or deadlines. Follow the attached example’s tone and keep the update under 250 words.
 
Google says personal-account Gems will automatically transition to skills from November 2026. 
Skills are reusable instructions available inside ordinary chats, so the work you put into a clear brief remains useful.

——
 4. Give your Research a Home 

NotebookLM is now Gemini Notebook, still a standalone research product with notebooks accessible across the Gemini ecosystem. 

• Open Gemini Notebook, create a notebook for one project, and select Add sources. 

• Bring together the relevant reports, Google Docs, PDFs, and links. 

• Select the sources you want included when asking a question. Source guide

 Using these sources, prepare me for [MEETING/DECISION]. Identify three points of agreement, meaningful contradictions, and unanswered questions. Cite the supporting passages. Keep your interpretation separate from what the documents explicitly say. 

Keep notebooks focused. A project brief, its latest research, and recent meeting notes give you a clearer working collection than an indiscriminate document dump.
——-

5. Use Deep Research with a Destination in Mind 

• Choose Deep Research, select your sources, and inspect the proposed plan before starting. 

• Google Search is included by default; connected Gmail, Drive, uploaded files, and notebooks can also contribute. 

• You can deselect Search when the task should stay within your chosen material. 

 Research [QUESTION] so I can decide [DECISION]. Use my attached requirements alongside current external evidence. Compare the viable options, identify the strongest objection to each, and finish with what remains unverified. Keep the report under 700 words. 

——-
 6. Use Gemini Inside the Documents you’re Working On 

If your account includes Gemini in Docs, open the document and select Ask Gemini. 

• The side panel can work with the document and reference other files or emails, reducing the need to move context between windows. 

• Access requires an eligible plan or supported experimental programme. G

 Review this project brief against [REFERENCE FILE]. Identify commitments that conflict, dates that differ, and questions the brief leaves unanswered. Suggest edits without adding unsupported claims. 

This is particularly useful for checking a proposal against the material it was built from..

——-
 7. Turn a Useful Prompt into a Routine 

Once a briefing works well, ask Gemini to schedule it. 

• Schedules are rolling out to personal accounts and are available to qualifying Workspace accounts; connected-app tasks require those apps to be connected. 

 Every weekday at 8:30 a.m. [TIMEZONE], review today’s Calendar and recent Gmail messages about [PROJECT]. Give me upcoming commitments, deadlines explicitly mentioned, and three items worth reviewing. Include source links. Don’t change my calendar. 

Check the schedule Gemini creates. Scheduled responses are prepared ahead of delivery, so they suit morning briefs better than live price monitoring.

——-
 🔖 When is Paying Worthwhile? 

Start with the access you already have. Consider an upgrade when you regularly hit limits or need specific features inside Google’s apps. 

Google currently offers AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra, with different allowances and benefits. Check the current plan comparison against the workflow you actually use. Happy Automating!

💸 MSCI Is Dropping Strategy. Does Bitcoin Pay For It? 💸 

Yesterday, MSCI named Strategy as one of five companies it plans to remove from its indexes. Strategy responded by stating that this would have little effect on its business. On the immediate mechanics, it has a point: index funds selling MSTR doesn’t force the company to sell bitcoin. 

The concern is what happens afterwards. Selling pressure could shrink the premium that helps Strategy finance its bitcoin purchases. Once you count its debt and preferred shares, Strategy's stock trades only a little above the value of its 848,250 BTC. When that premium disappeared over the summer, the company became a seller.

So, who else is on MSCI's list, how much forced selling are we talking about, and could any of it reach bitcoin itself? To find out, we went through MSCI's rulebook and Strategy's weekly SEC filings, then priced ten treasury companies ourselves.

 ❓ Who's On The List 

MSCI's new rule targets what it calls "non-operating companies", meaning businesses that mostly hold a pile of assets rather than run an operating business. 

If less than half of a company's assets are used in actual operations, MSCI puts it through five financial tests, such as how much it spends on running a business and how much of its funding goes into piling up assets. A company that fails four of the five is no longer eligible.

In case you're wondering, this isn't aimed at crypto alone. Yellow Cake, one of the five deletions, is a company that holds physical uranium, and Skel is an Icelandic investment firm. The other three hold bitcoin or Solana.

 📝 Marked for deletion : Strategy, Metaplanet, Upexi, Yellow Cake and Skel. Strategy alone accounts for 93.6% of the five's combined value in MSCI's indexes.

 📝 On the watchlist : 17 companies, including SharpLink, DeFi Development, Solana Company, SUI Group, TON Strategy and France's Capital B.

 📝 Not on the list at all : BitMine, Strive and Twenty One.

Existing index members are only removed if they fail the tests in two annual reports in a row, which is why most of the crypto names sit on the watchlist for now. To be clear, this is a preliminary list. MSCI confirms the final version on 11 November, and the changes take effect at the close on 30 November.

 🧐 How Much Selling Are We Talking About? 

Well, less than the headlines suggest. Strategy says funds tracking the affected MSCI indexes hold about 13 million of its shares, roughly 3.1% of the total. At the 15 October close of $151.29, that's around $2 billion, or about 60% of what MSTR trades on an average day. You'll still see JPMorgan's $2.8 billion estimate quoted, but that was made last November for MSCI's earlier proposal, which drew the line differently.

More importantly, index funds sell the shares. They don't touch Strategy's bitcoin, and whoever buys those shares on 30 November simply takes their place.

💸 Where Bitcoin Comes Into It 

That doesn't mean bitcoin is off the hook. You see, Strategy's whole model depends on its shares trading at a premium to the bitcoin it owns. As long as they do, it can sell new shares, use the cash to buy bitcoin and still leave each shareholder with more bitcoin per share than before. Once the premium goes, that trick stops working, and Strategy has to find another way to cover the roughly $15 billion of preferred stock and $6.8 billion of debt that sit on top of its bitcoin.

We got a preview of this over the summer. Apart from a token 32 BTC in late May, the selling began at the end of June, right as its premium disappeared once that debt and preferred stock are counted. By 9 August, its weekly filings showed 6,948 BTC sold for $431.8 million, at an average of about $62,150, mostly to pay preferred dividends and buy back its STRC preferred shares. When the share price recovered in late August, Strategy went straight back to buying and has since picked up 7,802 BTC at around $81,800 each. Put simply, it sold near the bottom and bought back roughly 30% higher.

As things stand, our numbers put Strategy at about 1.14x the value of its bitcoin on that same measure, or 0.91x if you leave the debt and preferred stock out. That's clear of the summer's danger zone, but short of the 1.22x Strategy said on its Q1 earnings call it needs for new shares to add bitcoin per share. If the index selling knocks the shares down far enough, it could end up back where it was in July. To be fair, it's better prepared this time, with a $4.88 billion USD Reserve set aside for dividends and interest and another $640 million in cash.

Metaplanet, the other bitcoin company on the deletion list, is in a tighter spot. Its shares trade at about 0.62x the value of its 44,000 BTC, and its bitcoin-backed loan stands at 17.7% of its holdings, well above the 10% guideline it set for itself.

 📊 How To Read A Treasury Company 

If you hold any of these stocks, here's what we'd keep an eye on.

 ➡️ Find out which mNAV someone is quoting. On the same day, Strategy comes out at 0.91x on the simple measure, 1.14x once debt and cash are included, and around 1.19x on the newer version shown on its own dashboard.

 ➡️ Look at what sits above the shareholders. Debt and preferred stock get paid first, and for Strategy that's roughly $22 billion combined.

 ➡️ Work out how long the cash lasts. The more months of dividends a company has set aside, the less likely it is to sell coins in a bad week.

 ➡️ Read the weekly filings yourself. Strategy files an 8-K on SEC.gov most Mondays, and a line that says "BTC Sold" tells you more than any headline.

 ➡️ Check MSCI's list each quarter, since a name on the watchlist today can be a deletion at the next review.

 ➖ ➖ ➖ ➖ 

 🧐 Bottom Line : The MSCI deletion is a one-off sale of roughly $2 billion of Strategy's shares, and its bitcoin isn't part of that trade. The risk to bitcoin comes later, if index selling pushes Strategy's premium back towards 1x and it has to choose between selling shares cheaply or selling bitcoin. This summer it chose bitcoin. If you hold MSTR or any other treasury stock, watch the final list on 11 November and the weekly filings after it, because a line that says "BTC Sold" matters far more than the index news.

BIS: Stablecoins and Bank Deposits Act as Substitutes as Deposit Hikes Slow Stablecoin Growth

BIS (Bank for International Settlements) working paper finds that stablecoins and bank deposits act as direct portfolio substitutes. Analyzing U.S. data, the authors show that a 1-basis-point hike in bank deposit rates cuts 10-week stablecoin market cap growth by roughly 3 percentage points (and up to ~9 percentage points under an IV approach). The substitution effect is significantly stronger for onshore-tied USDC (-4.8%) than offshore-centric USDT (-1.9%) and holds across bank CD rates and DeFi lending yields, demonstrating that traditional bank deposit pricing exerts an active drag on stablecoin growth. — link

🏁 Does A CME Listing Mark The Top? 🏁 

Bitcoin more than tripled in the seven weeks after CME announced its first bitcoin futures in 2017, then lost almost 60% in the three months after they launched. 

That timing gave crypto one of its favourite trading rules: when CME lists a coin, the top is in.

With Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap futures due to launch today, we checked whether the rule survives beyond its most famous example.

We looked at all nine coins CME had listed before today, using daily closes from Coinbase and cross-checking them against Bitstamp. We measured returns from announcement to launch, then 30 and 90 days afterwards. For the altcoins, we also compared returns with bitcoin over the same dates.

Because if a coin falls alongside the rest of the market, the listing may have little to do with it.

 🧐 How One Listing Became A Trading Rule 

CME announced bitcoin futures on 31 October 2017, when bitcoin was already up roughly sixfold that year. Trading began on 18 December, just after bitcoin peaked.

The timing was striking enough that San Francisco Fed economists later argued it “does not appear to be a coincidence”. Their explanation: futures made it easier for pessimists to bet against bitcoin, bringing selling pressure to a market previously dominated by buyers.

But that launch also broke new ground. Alongside Cboe’s debut a week earlier, it opened a regulated futures market to institutional traders.

Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap will be CME’s tenth and eleventh coins. Seven of those eleven arrived this year. There is less reason to expect each new contract to reshape trading the way bitcoin futures might have in 2017.

 📊 What Happened After The Other Listings? 

Our Coinbase and Bitstamp calculations agreed within 0.25 percentage points on every return except bitcoin in 2017, when Coinbase traded at a premium.

Here’s what the numbers showed:

 ➡️ After 30 days, the results looked weak. Six of nine coins were lower, Solana was flat, and the median return was −2.9%. But six of the eight altcoins finished within roughly five percentage points of bitcoin’s return. Most moved broadly with the market.

 ➡️ After 90 days, six of nine were higher. Cardano’s 0.4% gain and Stellar’s 0.6% were closer to flat. The three losers were bitcoin in 2017, Avalanche and Sui.

 ➡️ Ether was the clearest counterexample. It nearly tripled between the December 2020 announcement and the February 2021 launch, then gained another 143% over the following three months. Selling at launch meant missing most of that next leg up.

 ➡️ Avalanche and Sui fell sharply, but so did bitcoin. They lost 32% and 27% in the 90 days after their May 2026 launch. Bitcoin fell 20% over the same period. Both underperformed, though the broader sell-off explains a substantial part of their losses.

We also checked how common three-month declines were outside these events. Across the available price histories since 2017, the median coin fell in 53% of rolling 90-day windows. After a CME listing, only three of nine fell.

Those figures aren’t directly comparable enough to establish a trading edge. But they offer little support for the idea that CME launches reliably precede a decline.

🔍 So Is There Any Pattern At All? 

The strongest hint was in performance against bitcoin.

Five of the eight altcoins underperformed bitcoin over the 90 days after launch, with the median trailing by nine percentage points.

That’s worth noting. It’s also hard to separate from the broader weakness in altcoins against bitcoin. Eight cases cannot tell us whether CME listings contributed to that underperformance or simply happened during it.

The supposed pre-listing pump was inconsistent too.

Bitcoin and ether rallied hard before their launches, both during strong bull markets. But Cardano, Chainlink and Stellar each fell more than 30% between their January announcements and February launches.

Today’s pair offers no obvious shared pattern either. Since CME’s 22 September announcement, Uniswap is down 20%, bitcoin is down 5%, and Bitcoin Cash is up 3%.

There hasn’t been a broad listing rally to unwind.

 ❓ How To Read A “Sell The News” Claim 

These results are a useful reminder to ask a few questions before treating a familiar story as a trading rule:

 📝 How many examples support it? Bitcoin’s 2017 peak is memorable. The eight listings since have produced very different outcomes.

 📝 What did the rest of the market do? A 30% decline means something different when bitcoin also fell 20%. The underperformance matters, but the entire loss cannot reasonably be pinned on the listing.

 📝 How often does this happen anyway? If three-month declines are common throughout a coin’s history, a decline after a launch tells us little on its own.

 📝 What actually changed? Opening bitcoin’s first regulated futures markets was a bigger development than adding another coin to an established exchange.

 📝 Was there a rally beforehand? A “sell the news” explanation is less convincing when the coin was already falling before launch.

 ➖ ➖ ➖ ➖ ➖ 

 🔖 Bottom Line : The CME-top theory owes much of its reputation to December 2017. Across the nine listings we examined, the results were mixed, market conditions explained much of the movement, and six coins were higher three months later. That doesn’t make today’s launch a buy signal for Bitcoin Cash or Uniswap. It means the evidence is too weak to treat a CME listing, by itself, as a reason to sell.

Everything You Need To Know About Indonesia’s MSCI Crisis   

Indonesia just had its worst week in a generation, facing a risk of getting dropped from global stock indexes that guide trillions of dollars of investment. The stock market bled following the news, so allow us to explain what’s going on.  👇 

 🤔 What Happened? 

On October 15, MSCI told Indonesia that it no longer deserved the “emerging market” status and proposed skipping the “frontier” tag to move the country down to “standalone”. 

MSCI said that even a frontier label would understate how serious the problems are. 

On Friday, October 16, the Jakarta Composite fell more than 11% , its biggest one-day drop since 1998. By Monday’s close it had lost 14.8% across the two sessions. That’s about $82 billion in market value. ❗️ 

Both Bloomberg and Reuters reported that the two-session drop was deeper than anything during the Asian financial crisis. 

 What is “standalone” and why is it so serious?  

Standalone markets sit outside both MSCI’s emerging-market and frontier-market indexes. 

 ✌🏽 Two things will happen if Indonesia ends up getting downgraded.  

 ➡️ Passive funds that track those indexes would have to sell their Indonesian shares.

 ➡️ Active managers' measures against those indexes could also cut their holdings. 

Not only would Indonesia sit in the same group as Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine but also be the first standalone market in Asia. 

 Root Problem 

The core issue is “free float”, the share of a company’s stock available for the public to trade. 

Indonesia requires listed companies to float only 7.5% of shares and some billionaires own as much as 92.5% of their companies. 

 This results in more than 200 listed stocks with a free float rate below 15%.  

When fewer shares change hands, prices are easier to push around. MSCI pointed at two problems: unclear ownership structures and suspected coordinated trading.

🚀 SpaceX + Tesla: What a $3.5 Trillion Merger Would Mean 🚀 

Elon Musk likes the idea of merging SpaceX and Tesla. Now comes the harder part: agreeing on terms shareholders will accept.

On Tuesday’s SpaceX earnings call, Musk called a merger “a good idea”. Both boards have formed independent committees to explore it at shareholders’ request, but there’s no agreement yet. Musk himself warned that treating a deal as certain would be “overstating it”.

Together, the companies were worth roughly $3.5 trillion at Tuesday’s close. eToro’s Josh Gilbert says a combination would be the largest merger the market has ever seen. SpaceX rose about 8% in extended trading; Tesla gained 1.8%.

 🤖 The Surprise Is What Tesla Would Be Joining 

SpaceX’s biggest revenue source is now AI.

Its Q3 revenue jumped 161% to $14.58 billion, with AI contributing $7.56 billion—more than half. Most of that came from renting data-centre capacity to Anthropic, Google and Reflection AI, rather than selling access to its own models.

That changes how investors should think about this deal. Tesla shareholders would be buying into a business that now earns more from AI computing than from its other operations combined.

 💡 What Tesla Shareholders Need to Know 

 1️⃣ The terms matter more than the headline. 

There’s no offer price, exchange ratio or timetable. Until those exist, a $3.5 trillion combined valuation tells you little about what Tesla holders would actually receive.

Barclays and RBC expect an all-stock deal, meaning shareholders would likely receive SpaceX shares rather than cash. The value would depend on how many shares they get and what those shares are worth at closing.

 2️⃣ Analysts have very different ideas about the price. 

Tesla closed Tuesday at $373.71. RBC models an offer of $480 a share, roughly 28% higher, giving Tesla holders 48% of the combined company.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co thinks approval would require around $550, a 47% premium. These are analyst estimates, not offers—and any premium could narrow before closing.

🧹 Use AI to clean up your Digital life 

Your Downloads folder has become a filing cabinet with no drawers. Your phone is full of screenshots you meant to revisit. Your TV still has streaming apps from subscriptions you cancelled.

AI can make these chores easier by identifying what matters, organising the mess, and helping you set up maintenance that keeps running.

On phones, tablets and TVs, much of the useful AI automation comes from built-in settings that AI helps you configure.

These 5 prompts work across assistants. Give yours screenshots or a typed list, include your device model and software version, and share only the information needed. 👇 

——
 1. Turn Downloads into a folder you can actually use 

In a detailed firsthand account, writer Karen Spinner reported using Claude Cowork to sort 2,101 files into 11 main folders, rename confusing files and identify old installers for possible deletion. That is an individual result, but it shows what a well-scoped task can achieve. Read her walkthrough.

 Start here : Back up the originals, then test on a copied folder containing non-sensitive files. If your assistant supports local file access, grant access only to that test folder. Otherwise, provide a file list for a proposed organisation plan.
The prompt:

 “Help organise [FOLDER] around how I retrieve things: [BY PROJECT / CLIENT / PURPOSE]. First inspect what you can actually access and propose no more than six main folders. Show example moves before changing anything. After approval, move files without deleting, overwriting or changing their contents. Put ambiguous items in ‘Needs Review’ and keep a record of original and new locations. If you cannot access files, give me the plan only.”
 
——
 2. Reclaim photo storage without making AI choose your memories 

Photo cleanup involves two different decisions: which images you want to keep, and which originals need to live on the device.

AI can help organise the review. Your photo app is better placed to manage its own library.
Start here: Share your storage breakdown and photo-backup settings. Then choose the relevant route:

The prompt:

 “I use [DEVICE] and [PHOTO SERVICE]. Here are my storage and backup settings. Help me recover device space while preserving the photos I want. Separate local-copy removal, duplicate review and permanent deletion. Explain what each action changes in the cloud and on other devices. Prioritise storage optimisation, then help me review screenshots and large videos. Never assume similar-looking photos are duplicates or that old photos are unwanted.” 

——
 3. Put unused apps and temporary files on a maintenance routine 

The useful question is what occupies significant space, and can you recover it without losing something you need?

 Start here: Open your device’s storage screen and share the largest categories with your assistant. Mention apps and downloads you need when travelling or offline.
The prompt:

 “Here is the storage breakdown for [DEVICE AND SOFTWARE VERSION]. I want to recover approximately [AMOUNT] without losing personal data. Rank the three best opportunities using the sizes shown; don’t invent savings. Distinguish app size from app data, and downloaded media from originals. Explain what can be restored and what requires internet access. Then guide me through a built-in automatic maintenance option supported by this device.” 

——

4. Reduce browser and startup clutter 

Some clutter consumes attention and working memory rather than disk space: abandoned tabs, unnecessary extensions and apps that launch whenever you sign in.

 Start here: Provide your browser’s extension list and your computer’s startup-app list. Explain which tools you rely on.

The prompt:

 “Review these browser extensions and startup apps for [DEVICE/BROWSER]. Group them into ‘keep’, ‘consider disabling’ and ‘needs investigation’, with a reason for each. Don’t judge unfamiliar software by its name alone. Preserve security, backup, accessibility and password-management tools. Recommend reversible changes first, explain how to undo them, and show me any built-in setting that automatically reduces background resource use.” 

——
 5. Give your smart TV a cleanup matched to its actual model 

TV menus vary enough that generic instructions can send you looking for settings that do not exist.

Here, AI’s useful role is translating the manufacturer’s instructions into a short walkthrough. Treat this as guided cleanup unless your assistant has a verified device-control integration.

 Start here: Find the model number in the TV’s settings and photograph its storage or app-management screen.

The prompt:

 “My TV or streaming device is [BRAND, EXACT MODEL, SOFTWARE VERSION, COUNTRY]. Here is its storage screen. Find the manufacturer’s instructions for this model and link them. Help me review unused apps and clear cache where supported. Explain the difference between clearing cache and clearing app data before proceeding. Preserve my accounts and settings; exclude factory resets. Give me one step at a time and wait for the next screen.” 

Start with whichever device causes the most friction. Record its available storage before and after, save the instructions that worked, and let the supported maintenance settings handle the recurring chores.

👾 The AI Bug Hunter 👾 

It's been a grim week for anyone who runs a website.

Security researchers disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the open-source language W3Techs reckons sits behind 70% of all websites, which between them let an attacker run code on a web server without logging in. Collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, both carry a severity score of 9.2 out of 10, and Wiz says every PHP release of the past decade is affected by at least one, going back to PHP 5.4. Everything built on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla is in scope.

A fix landed on 21st October. Notably, plenty of teams are finding it takes longer to work out how much of their network runs PHP than to deploy the patch.

 ❓ Why Everyone Went Offline 

 ➡️ The NSA told organisations that couldn't update immediately to "take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," and the UK's NCSC said much the same.

 ➡️ Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi asked every website owner in the country to act that night. Mizuho's banking and securities arms, Shizuoka Bank and parts of MUFG suspended online services, while ANA, Japan Airlines and East Japan Railway pulled web services as a precaution.

 ➡️ Several European governments took public-facing sites down before the fix shipped.

Both bugs involve PHP mishandling a request that goes wrong, one around an out-of-memory condition, the other around internal state surviving after the memory it pointed to was freed. A later request can hit that stale state, and a server process tends to be holding passwords, session tokens and API keys from earlier activity, so reading those bytes does damage on its own.

That said, the advisories rate attack complexity as high and list conditions that have to be in place, so this isn't one request and every PHP site falls over.

 🤖 How It Surfaced 

The first signs of one bug showed up in 2024, during an external audit led by Quarkslab. A possible exploit was theorised, though nobody could pin down a concrete attack path, and every proposed fix carried compatibility or performance trade-offs the team couldn't choose between. Work stalled and restarted for months, and the PHP Foundation has called that a structural failure of its own process and resourcing.

What changed this year is that several AI-assisted teams worked out how to execute the attack. Wiz says building the exploit meant chaining bugs together and adapting to each target's memory layout, and that with frontier models in the loop, one researcher managed in a week what would otherwise have taken a world-class team months.

 🔑 Then Railway 

Also on 21st October, cloud platform Railway disclosed that an unauthorised party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and in some cases the decrypted contents. It has paused deployments and told everyone to rotate secrets, and believes the breach is part of a wider campaign against platform companies, aimed at compromising AI inference providers.

That matters because Railway is popular with indie developers and crypto builders, and environment variables are where people keep database passwords, API keys and sometimes wallet private keys. Investigator Taylor Monahan has linked roughly $371,000 in drains across at least 19 EVM chains to keys stored there, with the first theft landing at 19:36 UTC, over two hours before Railway went public.

 ➖ ➖ ➖ ➖ 

 🔖 Bottom Line : As of 22nd October, Germany's BSI, the Dutch cyber agency, CISA and Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary have yet to confirm a single successful PHP2Shell exploitation, and BSI's vice president says the bugs look harder to exploit than his team expected. Granted, exposure of this kind takes weeks to surface. If you run anything that accepts web requests, an old marketing site or internal dashboard included, patch it, then go looking for evidence of compromise rather than assuming the update erased it. The NCSC suggests keeping web-server and PHP logs from 17 October on. And if you've ever deployed on Railway, rotate every key and treat any private key that sat there as burnt. Stay safe out there.
